title: Shade and the city
bodyMd:
Over the past decade, several mid-sized European cities have announced targets for urban tree canopy: the share of a city's land area covered by tree crowns when seen from above. The appeal is easy to see. A mature street tree lowers the surface temperature of the pavement beneath it by several degrees on a summer afternoon, and canopy is cheap compared with most climate-adaptation spending.

Yet a canopy target stated as a single city-wide percentage can be met in ways that do little for the residents most exposed to heat. Planting is cheapest where land is already public and open: parks, riverbanks and school grounds. These sites are often in neighbourhoods that are already among the coolest, while the hottest districts tend to be dense, paved and short of space in which roots can spread. A city that raises its canopy from 18 to 25 per cent by planting along a river park may report success while the temperature on its most crowded streets is unchanged.

Some planners therefore argue for targets set street by street, or for weighting new planting by measured heat exposure. Critics reply that such targets are expensive to monitor, and that trees in narrow streets need costly soil cells beneath the pavement to survive. Both points are fair, but the first is weakening: satellite surface-temperature data is now available at a resolution fine enough to compare individual blocks, at almost no cost to a municipality.

The deeper difficulty is time. A sapling planted this year will not cast meaningful shade for fifteen to twenty years, and its survival depends on watering and maintenance budgets that are often the first to be cut. A target measured by trees planted rewards the ribbon-cutting; a target measured by canopy that still exists in twenty years rewards the maintenance that nobody photographs.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage, with no figure or table, about city targets for tree canopy. It says canopy cools pavements cheaply; that a single city-wide percentage can be met by planting in parks and riverbanks, which are often in already cool neighbourhoods, without cooling the hottest dense districts; that planners propose street-by-street or heat-weighted targets, which critics call expensive to monitor and costly because narrow streets need soil cells, though the monitoring objection is weakening because fine-grained satellite temperature data is now nearly free; and that saplings take fifteen to twenty years to give shade, so a target counting trees planted rewards ribbon-cutting while one counting canopy surviving in twenty years rewards maintenance.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set. It is not adapted from any published article, test item or Bocconi material, and names no real study, city or firm.
